title: Motion as a Token Layer, Not a Collection of Animations
content:
Without a system, every component invents its own duration and easing, transitions feel inconsistent, and design and engineering have no shared vocabulary. A motion system makes animation decisions as deliberate and as governed as colour or type.

WHAT A MOTION SYSTEM CONTAINS:
1. DURATION TOKENS — a small named scale.
2. EASING TOKENS — named curves mapped to semantic use.
3. CHOREOGRAPHY RULES — stagger, coordination, sequence limits, direction.
4. REDUCED-MOTION POLICY — handled at system level, not per component.
5. MOTION PRINCIPLES — 3–5 statements that adjudicate future decisions.
6. A LIST OF WHAT DOES NOT ANIMATE — as explicit as the list of what does.

WHERE IT LIVES: as Figma variables (motion variables can drive easing and timing, with modes), as CSS custom properties or platform tokens in code, and in the same export pipeline as colour and spacing. Motion tokens that are not in the token pipeline are documentation, not a system.

THE TEST OF WHETHER YOU HAVE ONE: pick two components at random and compare their transition durations. If they differ without a reason anyone can state, you have animations, not a system.

START SMALL. Four to six durations and five easings covers almost everything. Add a token only when a genuine new use case does not fit an existing one — the failure mode of motion systems is 14 durations nobody can distinguish.

title: Duration Tokens — A Working Scale
content:
| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `duration-instant` | 50ms | Changes that must feel immediate — checkbox tick, toggle, hover colour |
| `duration-fast` | 100ms | Small element transitions — tooltip appear, chip dismiss, focus ring |
| `duration-normal` | 200ms | The default for most transitions — dropdown open, tab switch, accordion |
| `duration-moderate` | 300ms | Medium elements — modal entry, panel slide, card expand |
| `duration-slow` | 400ms | Page-level transitions, multi-element choreography |
| `duration-deliberate` | 600ms | Intentionally paced high-emphasis moments — onboarding reveal, transaction confirmed |

RULES FOR APPLYING THEM:
- The default is `duration-normal`. If a component's animation needs a different token, there should be a stated reason.
- EXITS take the next token down from their entrance. Modal in at `moderate` (300ms), out at `normal` (200ms).
- FREQUENCY caps duration. Anything a user triggers more than a few times per minute gets `instant` or `fast`, regardless of how good the longer version looks in isolation.
- DISTANCE nudges duration up sub-linearly, and never past `slow` for in-viewport movement.
- `deliberate` requires justification in writing. It is for moments where slowness is the message — money moved, a record was created, something irreversible completed.

DO NOT create tokens for values you cannot tell apart. If nobody in a blind test can distinguish 200ms from 250ms in your product, you do not need both.

title: Easing Tokens — Named Curves and Their Semantics
content:
| Token | Curve | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `ease-standard` | cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) | Most UI transitions — elements moving between states |
| `ease-decelerate` | cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1) | Elements ENTERING the screen |
| `ease-accelerate` | cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 0.3) | Elements LEAVING the screen |
| `ease-spring` | spring, or cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) | Playful or tactile — FAB expand, drawer, like animation |
| `ease-linear` | linear | Looping animations ONLY — spinners, shimmer, progress, marquee |

THE THREE-CURVE MINIMUM: enter with decelerate, exit with accelerate, move within the viewport with standard. Ninety percent of a product's motion is covered by these three, and getting only this right removes most of what makes interfaces feel cheap.

WHY THE ASYMMETRY: an entering element should arrive and settle, so it decelerates. A leaving element should commit and go, so it accelerates. Reversing them makes entrances feel reluctant and exits feel hesitant — a subtle wrongness users feel and cannot name.

SPRINGS VS CURVES: springs have no fixed duration; they run until they settle. They read as physical and are the native idiom on iOS. Use them where the element should feel like an object with mass. Use bezier curves where you need a guaranteed duration — anything sequenced against something else.

FIGMA MAPPING: `ease-decelerate` ≈ Ease out, `ease-accelerate` ≈ Ease in, `ease-standard` ≈ Ease in and out, `ease-spring` ≈ the Gentle/Quick spring presets. Custom Bezier when you need the exact production curve. Bind these as motion variables so the prototype and the build cannot drift.

title: Reduced Motion — A System-Level Requirement
Motion Performance — What Is Cheap and What Is Not
content:
THE ONLY TWO CHEAP PROPERTIES on the web are `transform` (translate, scale, rotate) and `opacity`. Both are composited on the GPU without triggering layout or paint.

EXPENSIVE, IN ORDER OF PAIN:
- `width` / `height` / `top` / `left` / `margin` / `padding` — trigger LAYOUT on every frame. Animating these on a list reflows the page 60 times a second.
- `box-shadow`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, `border-radius` — trigger PAINT. Background blur is the single most expensive common effect.
- Animating many elements at once, regardless of property.
- Animating anything large — a full-viewport element scaling is expensive even as a transform.

RULES:
- Translate instead of moving with `top`/`left`. Scale instead of animating `width`/`height`.
- To fake a shadow change, cross-fade the opacity of a second element that already has the target shadow.
- `will-change: transform` sparingly and remove it after — it allocates GPU memory permanently while set.
- Never animate anything during initial page load. It competes with parsing and hurts LCP, and layout-affecting animation causes CLS. Both are Core Web Vitals and both correlate with conversion.
- Test on the slowest device in your support matrix, throttled. A mid-range Android from three years ago is the real target, not your laptop.

WHY THIS IS A DESIGN CONSTRAINT, NOT AN ENGINEERING ONE: if you design a card that expands by growing its height with an animating shadow, you have specified something that will jank. Designing it as a scale-and-cross-fade instead is a design decision with the same visual result and a tenth of the cost. Knowing which is which is part of the job.

title: Mapping Figma Motion to Code
content:
CSS TRANSITIONS — for simple state changes, hover, focus.
`transition: opacity var(--duration-normal) var(--ease-decelerate), transform var(--duration-normal) var(--ease-decelerate);`
Figma equivalent: a Smart animate transition with one duration and one easing. Limitation: no stagger, no per-property timing beyond listing them separately, no interruption control.

CSS KEYFRAMES — for looping and multi-step animation with no interaction.
Figma equivalent: a Figma Motion timeline. `@keyframes` map almost one-to-one to keyframe tracks. Dev Mode's Motion tab exports this directly.

WEB ANIMATIONS API — when you need to interrupt, reverse, or scrub in JS.
Figma equivalent: On drag interactions and scrubbable Motion timelines. This is what you specify when you want 'the dismissal reverses from its current position'.

MOTION.DEV / FRAMER MOTION (React) — the standard for product UI animation. Springs, layout animation, gesture following, enter/exit orchestration via `AnimatePresence`, and `staggerChildren`. Figma Motion exports React/motion.dev code directly from Dev Mode, which makes this the shortest path from timeline to build.

SPRING PARAMETER TRANSLATION: Figma's custom spring uses stiffness / damping / mass; the Plugin API exposes `physicalSpringToNormalized()` to convert those into Motion's normalised `bounce` value. motion.dev takes `stiffness`, `damping`, `mass` directly. The numbers are not universally interchangeable across libraries — hand over the parameters AND a reference recording, then expect one tuning pass in code.

SHOPIFY / LIQUID CONTEXT: Horizon and Dawn themes ship CSS custom properties for transitions. Prefer extending the theme's existing motion variables over adding your own, and keep everything to transform and opacity — theme performance scores are graded and the storefront's motion budget is genuinely small.

title: Motion Spec Template — What to Hand Over
content:
For each animated element:

ELEMENT: cart drawer
TRIGGER: click on 'Add to cart', or click on cart icon
PROPERTIES: transform translateX 100% → 0; scrim opacity 0 → 0.5
DURATION: 300ms (`duration-moderate`) in, 200ms (`duration-normal`) out
EASING: `ease-decelerate` in, `ease-accelerate` out
STAGGER: scrim starts at 0ms, drawer at 0ms, line items stagger 40ms each starting at 120ms, max 5 staggered then remainder together
INTERRUPTIBLE: yes — dismissal reverses from the current position, does not queue
REDUCED MOTION: no translate; scrim and drawer cross-fade at 0.01ms (effectively instant)
WHAT MUST NOT ANIMATE: the line-item quantity numbers, the subtotal value
INFORMATIONAL OR DECORATIVE: informational — communicates that the drawer came from the right and can be dismissed there
PERFORMANCE NOTE: transform and opacity only; do not animate width

WHY EACH LINE EXISTS: the exit and the reduced-motion variant are the two most commonly omitted, and the two most commonly wrong in the build. 'What must not animate' prevents an engineer from helpfully adding a number-count animation to a subtotal. 'Interruptible' is invisible in any prototype and is the difference between a drawer that feels responsive and one that feels stuck.

WHERE IT LIVES: Dev Mode annotations on the element, plus the Motion tab if authored in Figma Motion. Not a separate document — motion specs in separate documents are not read.

title: Motion Personality — Making Motion Say Something
content:
Motion is one of the few brand surfaces users feel without noticing. Two products with the same layout and the same colours feel completely different if one moves at 150ms with tight easing and the other at 400ms with springs.

THE FOUR DIALS:
- SPEED. Fast (120–200ms) reads as efficient, professional, tool-like — Linear, Arc, trading interfaces. Slow (350–600ms) reads as considered, premium, calm — Headspace, luxury retail, wellness.
- BOUNCE. Zero overshoot reads as serious and precise. Overshoot reads as friendly and playful. Financial products earn trust with zero; consumer apps earn affection with some.
- SCALE OF MOVEMENT. Small travel (4–12px) reads as refined. Large travel and full-screen transforms read as expressive and confident, and cost more performance.
- SIMULTANEITY. Everything at once reads as snappy. Choreographed stagger reads as crafted and slightly ceremonial.

MATCHING IT TO CONTEXT:
- SHOPIFY / retail: fast and near-zero bounce on anything in the purchase path — every millisecond is measurable friction. Save expressive motion for brand moments outside the funnel (hero, story sections, post-purchase).
- CRYPTO / fintech: fast, precise, zero bounce, and absolutely no motion on numbers. Motion's job is to communicate system state (pending → confirming → confirmed), and state transitions are the one place a deliberate pace earns trust because it maps to real elapsed time.
- AI products: motion carries the model's thinking. Streaming text, a settling response, a tool-use indicator. The temptation is to animate 'intelligence'; the better instinct is to animate STATUS honestly — the user's real question is 'is this working and how long will it take'.

WRITE THE DIALS DOWN as part of the motion principles. 'We move fast and do not bounce' resolves more future arguments than a page of prose.

title: Motion Critique Checklist
content:
PURPOSE
- Can you state in one sentence what each animation communicates? Answers that name a relationship (origin, causality, identity, status) pass; 'it feels premium' does not.
- Remove it: is the interface still comprehensible? If yes, it is decoration — allowed once per surface.

DIRECTION AND SEMANTICS
- Is the transition grammar consistent — forward always one way, back always the reverse?
- Does the transition type match the relationship (Smart animate for same-object, Push for siblings, overlay for on-top)?
- Do enter and exit use opposite directions and asymmetric durations?

TIMING
- Is every duration a token, or are there orphan numbers?
- Duration × frequency: how much of the user's day is this?
- Nothing over 500ms without a written reason.

CHOREOGRAPHY
- Is there a single lead element?
- Total staggered sequence under ~500ms?
- Shared easing within each semantic group?

ACCESSIBILITY
- Reduced-motion variant specified, with informational motion preserved?
- Nothing flashing more than 3 times per second?
- Focus is never moved or obscured by an animation?
- No motion required to understand a state change (motion is reinforcement, never the only channel)?

PERFORMANCE
- Transform and opacity only?
- Nothing animating during initial load?
- Tested on the slowest supported device?

COMPLETENESS
- Exit authored, not defaulted?
- Interruption behaviour specified?
- The list of what must NOT animate written down?
